title: Read like a writer
summary: Analyse what an original model paragraph is doing, reduce it to a reusable structural move and transfer that move to new material without copying its topic, wording or details.

sections.title: Read once for meaning and again for craft
content: A reader asks what a paragraph means. A writer also asks how the paragraph creates that meaning. The second reading looks beneath topic words and notices decisions: where the paragraph establishes its purpose, how evidence is ordered, what relationship joins each sentence and how the final line explains significance.

E7.1–E7.4 supplied the vocabulary for this analysis: paragraph promise, purposeful specifics, cohesion, direction and resolution. E7.5 combines them so that a strong model becomes a source of transferable craft rather than a sentence template to copy.

sections.title: Name the work each sentence performs
content: Read this original model: ‘At first, the repair-café volunteers tried to serve every visitor as soon as the doors opened. Tools disappeared between tables, and several repairs stopped while people searched for missing parts. The team then created three labelled tool stations and asked each table to return equipment after every job. Within an hour, the queues began moving steadily. The simple system did more than save time: it turned a crowded room into a shared process that newcomers could follow.’

A reverse outline names functions, not topics: initial approach → concrete problem and consequence → targeted response → observable result → wider significance. That sequence is the model’s reusable move. ‘Tools’, ‘tables’ and ‘queues’ belong only to this particular repair-café example.

sections.title: Notice how language serves the structure
content: The opening phrase ‘At first’ makes later change possible. ‘Tools disappeared’ turns a general difficulty into an observable problem, while ‘repairs stopped’ states its consequence. ‘The team then’ introduces a response at the exact point when the reader understands why it is needed.

The final sentence does not merely repeat that queues improved. It moves from the immediate result—saving time—to the significance: the new system made participation easier for newcomers. Cohesion follows the logic of the change rather than a stack of decorative connectors.

sections.title: Abstract before you transfer
content: Before writing about a new topic, remove the model’s nouns and record its decisions in neutral language: show an initial method; reveal a specific weakness and consequence; introduce a response designed for that weakness; report an observable result; explain why the change matters beyond the immediate result.

This abstract plan can guide a paragraph about reducing food waste, organising a study group or maintaining a garden. Copying ‘At first’, ‘three labelled stations’, ‘within an hour’ and ‘did more than’ would reproduce the model’s surface. Transferring the causal sequence preserves the craft while allowing the new evidence to determine the language.

sections.title: Let new evidence reshape the move
content: Transfer is adaptation, not substitution. For a food-waste paragraph, the initial weakness might be an undifferentiated bin that hid what students discarded. The response might be a short sorting audit followed by smaller serving options. The result and significance must come from that evidence; they should not imitate queues or newcomers merely because those appeared in the model.

A structural move may also need changing. If the new evidence has no reliable measured result, describe an observable change without inventing a number. If the most important insight is a contrast rather than a cause, reorganise the plan. The model offers one tested option, not a compulsory mould.

sections.title: Distinguish transfer from imitation
content: Classify a weak transfer as surface copying, noun substitution, borrowed evidence, structural mismatch or unsupported improvement. Noun substitution changes ‘tools’ to ‘trays’ while preserving every other sentence. Borrowed evidence invents three stations or a one-hour result because the model used them. Structural mismatch forces a problem–response sequence onto material that does not contain a meaningful change.

Repair the planning note before the prose. Write the model’s functions in one column and the new topic’s actual evidence in another. If a new detail cannot be justified independently of the model, remove it.

sections.title: Transfer the decision, not the sentence
content: Make six decisions about reverse outlining, structural abstraction, language choices, independent evidence, surface copying and an adapted model paragraph. Complete the group before viewing feedback.
